Trump administration plans $2.8 billion munitions sale to Israel, sources say

By Humeyra Pamuk
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:02 pm UTC
2 min read

By Humeyra Pamuk

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration is planning to sell to Israel a munitions package worth $2.8 ‌billion, which will include tens of thousands of highly ‌destructive 2,000-pound bombs, according to a U.S. official familiar with the sale.

The planned sale, ​which has been informally communicated to relevant congressional committees who weigh in on large arms sales, includes 20,000 MK 84s and 20,000 BLU-117s, the official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

News of the package ‌was first reported by ⁠the Washington Post.

The State Department and the Israeli embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

U.S. ⁠public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of ​voters and ​66% of Democrats believe the United ​States is too supportive of ‌Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.

The 2,000-pound bombs have been regularly used by Israel in Gaza as well as in Lebanon, drawing scrutiny from rights experts. More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, ‌according to Gaza health authorities. A U.N. ​inquiry determined that Israel had committed genocide ​in Gaza, a charge ​Isarel rejects.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Israel calls its actions self-defense, after Hamas-led militants killed ‌1,200 people and took more than ​250 hostages in ​an October 2023 attack.

The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28. Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel ​and Gulf states that ‌host U.S. bases. U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks ​in Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.

data.title: Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month, CBO says
data.description:
Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month, CBO says

By Jacob Bogage
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:01 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Jacob Bogage

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The six-month-old U.S. war against Iran has cost $38 billion so far and that amount is projected to rise by $3 billion a month, Congress' nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ‌ways to end the conflict and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz.

The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5% in ‌the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office accounting, which totaled expenses through August 1.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The mounting costs have strained U.S. munitions stockpiles and driven up energy ​prices, raising concerns about the country's ability to respond to other potential conflicts and adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.

The cost was close to the $37.5 billion that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reported at a Senate hearing on July 21.

The budget office said the majority of the costs stem from the rapid drawdown of munitions, estimating that it could take five years to replenish U.S. stockpiles. Reuters reported in August that the U.S. had ‌used "virtually all" of its long-range precision missiles during the ⁠war.

The Department of Defense did not cooperate with congressional financial auditors, CBO reported.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Representatives from the White House and Department of Defense did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The inquiry was conducted at the request of the ⁠top Democrat on the U.S. House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania.

"Donald Trump's disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded," Boyle said in a statement.

"Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American ​taxpayers ​tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Eighteen ​U.S. military service members have died in the Iran war.

The ‌report did not include costs of recent strikes on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on U.S. military installations in the region. It also did not factor in the borrowing expenses associated with financing the war, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.

IMPACT ON US READINESS

The CBO accounting found the war could have sprawling consequences for the U.S. defense posture and the domestic economy.

The deficit in critical munitions, including missile interceptors, risks hampering the Pentagon's response in the event of another major conflict, such as potential hostilities involving ‌China and Taiwan, CBO said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

At the July hearing in the Senate, Hegseth pleaded for ​nearly $90 billion emergency funding legislation to restock munitions supplies.

"Without these funds, we face critical ​shortfalls," Hegseth said.

Energy shocks caused by attacks in the Strait of ​Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil traveled before the war — and on ‌energy facilities in neighboring Gulf countries have sharply increased prices ​for consumers and global producers.

The rising ​cost of the war also threatens to weigh on deteriorating U.S. fiscal health. The nation's total public debt surpassed $40 trillion in August.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump regularly contrasts the Iran war with the U.S. invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan that followed the September 11, 2001, attacks.

The eight-year U.S. ​war in Iraq, which involved more than 100,000 ‌ground troops at its peak, cost $2 trillion, Reuters reported. The two-decade-long U.S. conflict in Afghanistan, which also involved more than 100,000 ​troops at its most intense, cost $2.3 trillion, according to Brown University's Costs of War project.

(Reporting by Jacob Bogage; Additional reporting ​by Idrees Ali; Editing by Colleen Jenkins, Don Durfee and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: Empty benches as schools reopen in Venezuela's quake-hit Guaira
data.description:
Empty benches as schools reopen in Venezuela's quake-hit Guaira

AFP News
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 5:51 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Schools in Venezuela's quake-scarred coastal state of La Guaira were deserted on Tuesday, a day after the start of the new school year, with many parents opting to keep children home for fear of further deadly tremors.

La Guaira, home to a popular resort of the same name 40 kilometers from Venezuela's capital Caracas, was devastated by powerful back-to-back quakes on June 24 that left over 6,500 people dead.

Dozens of schools were damaged in the worst disaster in the Caribbean country in decades, which reduced hundreds of buildings to rubble.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A further 60 schools were converted into shelters for thousands of people left homeless by the magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 quakes.

Amni Nunez, a 40-year-old industrial engineer sent his two young children back to school, arguing they "need to understand that the world keeps spinning and that we have to learn to live with this new reality."

But many parents were too fearful of a repeat disaster to allow their children back into the classroom.

Just over 300 students have enrolled for the new school year at John Paul II Diocesan Educational Unit, one of the few schools open in the port city of La Guaira.

The school has capacity for more than double that.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Only seven children attended class on Tuesday.

"The return to classes will be gradual and safe, focusing primarily on the emotional well-being not only of our students but also of our staff," the principal Marco Antonio Espinoza said.

He said it was "normal" to be afraid, given the hundreds of aftershocks recorded since the earthquakes, but said he was struck by the desire of the survivors "to live and carry on with their activities."

Yanet Dominguez, a fifth-grade teacher at the school, said parents had been plying her with questions about the building's structural safety.

"I told them yes, that improvements have been made to the building this year, and that they shouldn't be afraid to send their children," she said.

data.title: Sanders and Bannon call for AI limits as public unease grows
data.description:
Sanders and Bannon call for AI limits as public unease grows

By Courtney Rozen
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 5:54 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

"March on Washington 2026: Defend the Vote" rally and march for voting rights in Washington

1 of 2
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders (I–VT) speaks during the "March on Washington 2026: Defend the Vote" rally and march for voting rights in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 28, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

By Courtney Rozen

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Progressive U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a close ally of President Donald Trump, called on Tuesday for restrictions on AI systems, uniting two political adversaries around concerns that the technology will harm humans.

The two were due to appear at the same Washington gathering as concern ‌about AI's risks spreads beyond Washington and Silicon Valley.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Speaking first, Sanders, a self-described democratic socialist, warned about the "growing threat" of AI and said the industry needed to be ‌regulated with binding safety rules.

"AI has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and making it harder for our young people to enter the workforce."

He added, "As many scientists believe could happen, this technology ​will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences."

Sanders drew applause from the room when he criticized tech executives for centralizing control over AI technology, including SpaceX CEO and former Trump adviser Elon Musk.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Last month, we learned that AI has been used for the first time ever to create new viruses. In the wrong hands, this could lead to new bioweapons and a potential global pandemic that could lead to the deaths of tens of millions of people," Sanders said.

Bannon, a former White House strategist during Trump's first presidential term, has criticized Trump's approach to overseeing AI, placing the blame for the ‌president's unwillingness to regulate the technology squarely on tech companies. On ⁠his Monday podcast, Bannon said Congress should not pass laws that prohibit states from enforcing their own rules for the technology.

UNLIKELY BEDFELLOWS

The decision of Sanders and Bannon, who are on opposite ends of America's ideological divide, to speak at the same gathering on Tuesday underscores how concerns over AI ⁠and data centers are cutting across party lines and producing unlikely political bedfellows.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump on Monday downplayed concerns expressed by industry leaders over the weekend about the misuse of artificial intelligence harming people, saying the U.S. already has guardrails in place for the powerful technology.

Backing Trump's position on Tuesday, Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson said there cannot be a moratorium on artificial intelligence development without losing the competitive edge to China and ​that ​AI companies can regulate themselves.

"They can self-regulate. They don't need the government to tell them to slow it ​down. If they want to slow it down, they should," Johnson told ‌reporters.

The view that regulations will harm U.S. companies' ability to compete with their Chinese counterparts is shared by tech executives, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Recent surveys have found majorities of Americans worry the technology could be used to eliminate jobs, raise costs for families or otherwise cause social harm.

BACK FROM RECESS

The U.S. House of Representatives ended its long summer break on Monday, with members in the House and Senate holding private conversations about whether or not to legislate on AI, especially after Trump said there was no need for legislative action.

Congress has been criticized in the past for lacking the collective expertise to rein in or regulate technology companies.

Speaking to Reuters, Republican Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio said, "This process of legislating takes so long. Imagine AI four years ‌in. We're dealing with stuff that isn't even relevant in four years."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Residents in several states have also challenged ​proposals for new data centers, a critical component of the AI boom. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published in June, ​77% of Americans worry AI-driven data centers will raise electricity costs.

Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon ​captured public attention last week when he said he resigned from the company, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill ‌us all by the end of the decade."

Also on Tuesday, Andrew Ferguson, ​the chairman of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, expressed ​suspicions over AI companies seeking antitrust exemptions while they also lobby for new regulations.

Reuters previously reported that U.S. senators are debating a bill that would block states from enforcing their own laws governing certain risks posed by AI models. Previously, efforts to restrict state AI laws failed in the U.S. Senate.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Sanders and Bannon addressed the same event ​as AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler, who leads the largest federation of labor ‌unions in the U.S.

Sanders, along with House progressive Rep. Greg Casar, has called for the U.S. to pass legislation halting development of AI tools that are capable ​of "overthrowing or undermining the U.S. government," until the government creates a new agency to police the technology. Casar and Sanders have not released specifics.

(Reporting by Courtney ​Rozen. Additional reporting by Tim Reid and Richard Cowan. Editing by David Gregorio and Nick Zieminski)

data.title: Under pressure at home, Merz cancels UN appearance, source says
data.description:
Under pressure at home, Merz cancels UN appearance, source says

By Andreas Rinke
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 5:43 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Andreas Rinke

BERLIN, Sept 15 (Reuters) - German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will not go on a planned trip to New York next week, a government source said on Tuesday, as pressure mounts on him following electoral setbacks for ‌his conservative party.

Merz faces growing internal criticism following his Christian Democrats' (CDU) poor performance this month in Saxony-Anhalt, where the ‌far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came close to securing an outright majority in a state election.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Merz had been scheduled to attend the UN General Assembly in New York ​with other world leaders.

"Contrary to original plans, the chancellor will not travel to New York next week, as his presence is required in Berlin," the source said.

PRESSURE ON MERZ INTENSIFIES

At the national level, the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the CSU, are polling at between 18% and 20%, far below their result in last year's federal election and significantly behind the AfD.

Confidence in the chancellor has also weakened within ‌his own party. A weekend INSA poll found ⁠that a majority of CDU supporters no longer believe Merz is the right person for the job, while 78% of the wider public said the same.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Merz's conservatives have called a special meeting for Sunday, ⁠a party source said earlier on Tuesday.

The source said the aim of the meeting was to coordinate the party's response to votes this coming Sunday in the states of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, chart a course with support at a record low and demonstrate unity behind Merz's leadership.

After the ​setback in ​Saxony-Anhalt, some CDU critics have said another poor performance this weekend could ​intensify pressure on Merz.

Asked at an event with business ‌leaders whether poor outcomes in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin state polls could unseat him, Merz said he was determined to serve out his full four-year term.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Instead, he said the coalition with the centre-left SPD would pursue more reforms to solve Germany's problems.

MERZ PROMISES TO EASE FUEL COSTS

"I was elected for four years, and I would like us to use these four years to steer the country out of this difficult period," said Merz, adding that he did not want to resort to a vote of confidence to ‌push through his agenda.

He said he wanted, among other things, the European Union ​to strike more trade alliances, such as those with the MERCOSUR bloc, Mexico ​and Australia, as a counterweight to U.S. and Chinese economic ​dominance.

Merz also promised fuel cost relief measures for motorists burdened by a surge in oil prices, but ‌did not elaborate.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

At a separate event, CSU leader Markus ​Soeder said he was backing Merz ​and expected CDU leaders to do the same.

The CDU is polling at 7% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In Berlin, it is tied for the lead with the Left party at 20%.

Merz has rejected attemptsto tie his political future to individual state election ​results, arguing that Germany needs stability to push ‌through an ambitious reform agenda and navigate European challenges including acts of hybrid warfare and support for Ukraine.

He ​has said there are no obvious alternative leaders or policies.

(Reporting by Andreas Rinke and Miranda Murray, Writing by Friederike ​Heine and Ludwig Burger; Editing by Ros Russell and Timothy Heritage)

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Republican U.S. Representative Thomas Massie filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday, accusing him ‌of abusing his office by executing an order for hostilities against Iran ‌without approval by Congress.

"The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary's vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and ‌America first," Pentagon press secretary ⁠Kingsley Wilson said in an emailed statement.

Massie filed his articles of impeachment against Hegseth as privileged, meaning the House must take them ⁠up within two legislative days.

Massie, an outspoken critic of the war on Iran and aid to Israel, is not up for reelection. He lost his primary in May to a ​candidate backed ​by Republican President Donald Trump after Massie ​angered the president by leading a ‌push to release Justice Department files tied to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Massie was defeated by Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL backed by Trump and bolstered by heavy spending by pro-Israel groups.

Polls show the war that began with February 28 attacks on Iran by U.S. and Israeli forces is unpopular with voters. data.title: Judges question DOJ bid to revive cases against Trump foes Comey, James
data.description:
Judges question DOJ bid to revive cases against Trump foes Comey, James

By Andrew Goudsward
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 5:25 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Andrew Goudsward

RICHMOND, Virginia, Sept 15 (Reuters) - A U.S. appeals court on Tuesday appeared wary of the Justice Department's bid to revive criminal cases against two of President Donald Trump's longtime adversaries, former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

The prosecutions ‌of Comey and James, which a judge dismissed last year, were among the most high-profile instances of the Trump administration using federal law enforcement to ‌target perceived political enemies and generated upheaval inside the Justice Department.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But the arguments on Tuesday at the Richmond, Virginia-based 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals focused on the narrower issue of whether ​former Attorney General Pam Bondi had the authority to appoint Trump ally Lindsey Halligan as interim U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia to prosecute the cases.

Concerns over Halligan's appointment led a lower-court judge to throw out both cases in a significant blow to the Trump Justice Department. Whether the DOJ will be able to proceed hinges on differing interpretations of a federal appointments law that governs how temporary U.S. Attorney vacancies can be filled.

Two of the three judges on the appeals court panel ‌expressed skepticism that federal law authorized Halligan's appointment and empowered ⁠her to secure both indictments.

Chief U.S. Circuit Judge Albert Diaz said the Trump administration's interpretation of the law would allow the DOJ to make a "limitless" number of interim appointments for U.S. Attorneys, evading the Senate's authority to approve top federal prosecutors.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"How can ⁠that possibly be?" Diaz, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama, asked.

Justice Department lawyer Henry Whitaker said that while the law may give the government that authority, in practice it would not make sense for the department to rely on an "endless stream" of temporary officials.

Circuit Judge Henry Floyd suggested that without being properly appointed, Halligan was no different than any ​ordinary ​person when she secured the indictments.

"What's different with a man on the street?" Floyd asked.

The ​dispute arises from the circumstances of Halligan's September 2025 appointment ‌as interim U.S. Attorney after her predecessor, Eric Siebert, was ousted after expressing a reluctance to charge both Comey and James.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Siebert had previously served a 120-day interim stint, and U.S. District Judge Cameron McGowan Currie concluded that Bondi did not have the authority to make another temporary appointment. Currie determined that both cases had to be tossed because Halligan, a former personal lawyer to Trump with no prior prosecutorial experience, secured both indictments by herself.

Comey has since been charged in a separate federal case accusing him of threatening Trump in a social media post showing seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86-47." That case is continuing.

LEGAL ARGUMENTS ‌OVER APPOINTMENT AUTHORITY

Whitaker urged the appeals court to reject Currie's interpretation of the appointments law, ​arguing it would wrongly limit the attorney general's ability to name interim U.S. Attorneys to lead ​94 federal prosecutors' offices across the U.S.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Ephraim McDowell, a lawyer for Comey, ​warned that the DOJ's view would allow the president to indefinitely "install political allies as chief federal prosecutors."

The cases against James and Comey ‌were brought after Trump mentioned both by name in a ​September 2025 social media post demanding that ​Bondi, who was then attorney general, take action against his adversaries.

TRUMP'S HISTORY WITH COMEY AND JAMES

Trump fired Comey as FBI director during his first term as Comey was overseeing an investigation into potential ties between Trump's 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. James successfully sued Trump and his family business ​for fraud following his first term.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The indictment against Comey ‌accused him of lying to Congress about authorizing leaks to the news media. James was charged with bank fraud for allegedly misrepresenting ​her use of a Virginia home.

Both denied wrongdoing and alleged they were targeted with vindictive prosecutions as part of a Trump retribution campaign.

(Reporting ​by Andrew Goudsward in Richmond, Virginia; Editing by Matthew Lewis and Alistair Bell)

data.title: Desperate For A Job, I Applied At A Sandwich Shop. The Response I Got Was Soul-Crushing.
data.description:
Desperate For A Job, I Applied At A Sandwich Shop. The Response I Got Was Soul-Crushing.

Karen D. Garman
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 5:35 pm UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

I handed in a job application at a sandwich shop last week. There was a giant Now Hiring sign taped to the front window, so I walked in and, to my surprise, they handed me a paper application. I filled it out, smiled, and returned it to them.

They never called me.

Also Read: I Wanted My Daughter To Feel Welcome At School. Then Her Teacher Made A Decision That Shattered My Hopes.

I tell myself it's probably because I'm too old. Maybe it's because I didn't apply online, or because the kid behind the counter didn't scan my info into the system. I don't know. I only know that I was ready to make sandwiches for minimum wage, and nobody even wanted that from me.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

I have a master's degree in interdisciplinary arts and decades of experience, both personal and professional. I speak two languages. As if any of that matters.

I've been told all my life that I'm smart, and yet here I am, chronically underemployed, invisible in the job market, and applying anywhere I can — hardware stores, pet supply chains, and garden centers. No one writes back. No one calls.

"Please upload your résumé," I'm told. I do and it disappears into the algorithmic abyss, and I never hear from a human being.

Also Read: At 62, I Hadn't Been On A Date In Decades. Here's What Happened When I Tried The Apps.

I don't need a career. I need a paycheck. But the system seems to think I'm either aiming too low or not playing the game right, or worse, that I don't exist at all.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

This has been going on for years. I've rewritten my résumé more times than I can count, tried leaving off my degree, tried playing up my "people skills," tried the QR codes and portals and ghost-job listings that don't lead anywhere. Nothing works. Every rejection chips away at something I used to believe about myself. Something like worth.

At one point, I thought maybe I had undiagnosed ADHD. Or social anxiety. Or something that could explain the gap between what I know I can do and how the world seems to view me. But mostly, I return to one haunting possibility: Maybe I'm just clueless. Maybe I've been clueless for years, and everyone else knows it except me.

That is, hands down, my greatest fear — not failure, not poverty, not even loneliness: the idea that I might be fundamentally out of sync with the world, and not even aware of it.

Also Read: This Is The Single Most Valuable Free Resource In America — And Conservatives Want It Gone

Because here's the truth that nobody likes to talk about: being educated, competent and willing to work is no guarantee that you'll find work. Especially not in a system where hiring has become automated, impersonal and biased in a hundred tiny, invisible ways. Especially not in a country where being overqualified is treated like a liability, where aging disqualifies you from entry-level jobs, and where the tech used to "streamline" applications often ends up gatekeeping the people who need the job the most.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

I'm not homeless. I'm not addicted. I'm not mentally ill. I've never made more than $20,000 in a year, either. I'm somewhere in the gray area where you're struggling but not visibly enough to qualify for help. The kind of person nobody builds policy for. The kind of person nobody notices when they fall through the cracks, because we don't fit any of the typical narratives about success or failure.

I know work isn't just about money. It's also about rhythm, purpose and dignity. It gives your days structure and your brain something to do besides spiral into self-questioning. But when you're perpetually locked out of even the most basic opportunities, the effect isn't just economic. It's existential.

I know I'm not the only one. There are millions of us — smart, willing, even desperate to work — stuck in the liminal space between unemployment and invisibility. Nearly half of all college graduates are underemployed, many for a decade or more. Résumés vanish into algorithmic black holes, and being "overqualified" is often treated like a red flag. Older applicants, especially women, are routinely overlooked. It's not just me. It's a quiet crisis, and it's growing.

Also Read: I Gave Up My High-Profile NYC Job And Moved Home To Serve Ramen. It Changed My Life.

This piece may sound absurd to some people who believe success is tied to how hard a person tries, and failure indicates a flaw in someone's character, an inherent lack of discipline, or an unwillingness to go all out for what you want.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But what if the reality of success or failure is not dependent on a person's character but is simply the result of a person's circumstances, which are, ultimately, rarely within one's control?

Or what if the world has finally arrived in the digital age, and those of us still fumbling around in the world of history, philosophy, humanity and faith have become ... obsolete?

I used to think people like me would be the ones shaping the future. Now I'm just trying to survive in it. I was trained to think critically, to lead, to imagine better systems. But I'm being overlooked by people — and AI — who aren't capable of doing what I can do. They don't realize they're saying no to the very resources that could help us navigate the crises ahead.

Also Read: At 19, I Was Forced To Marry A Stranger And Was Sexually Assaulted Every Month For 12 Years

And if I can't do that, I just want a chance to be useful somehow.

Advertisement

Advertisement

I have so much to give.

I would make the best sandwiches anyone has ever tasted.

Karen D. Garman is a writer, artist and educator whose work explores trauma, transformation and the search for meaning in a fractured world. Her essays and hybrid narratives blend memoir, social critique and poetic language. She writes frequently about addiction recovery, neurodivergence, ecological consciousness and the edges of human connection. Karen is currently developing a contemporary art movement inspired by the Situationists and working on a hybrid literary novel.

data.title: Italian NATO jet downs suspected Russian drone over Lithuania
data.description:
Italian NATO jet downs suspected Russian drone over Lithuania

By Andrius Sytas, Tom Balmforth and Janis Laizans
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 5:30 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A NATO fighter jet shoots down a drone in Lithuania

1 of 2
Military police and response vehicles stand parked near the site where, according to the Lithuanian national crisis management centre, a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone near Pratkunai village, Lithuania, September 15, 2026, in this screengrab from a handout video. Lithuanian Army/Handout via REUTERS

By Andrius Sytas, Tom Balmforth and Janis Laizans

SIAULIAI AIR BASE, Lithuania, Sept 15 (Reuters) - An Italian fighter jet deployed on a NATO mission shot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace ‌on Tuesday that "most probably" came from Russia, Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said.

Lithuanian authorities said ‌on Tuesday they are still investigating the origin of the debris.

A Ukrainian military source told Reuters the debris in the images ​appeared to be from a Geran-2, a long-range attack drone widely used by Russia.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Russia did not immediately comment on the incident.

If confirmed, it would be the first known instance of a Russian military drone entering Lithuania, a NATO and European Union member, since the summer of 2025, when two Russian drones accidentally crashed in the ‌country.

The drone entered Lithuanian airspace from ⁠Belarus, a Russian ally, after midnight and was shot down near the southern village of Pratkunai not far from the city of Kaunas, the Lithuanian national crisis ⁠management centre said.

"Last night, again, the Italian pilots have intervened and they have shot down a threat that most probably came from Russia", Crosetto told reporters at Siauliai Air Base, where Italian fighters are based as part of the ​NATO Baltic ​Air Defence mission.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The presence of Italian aircraft here is ​the clear demonstration of the value of ‌the Atlantic alliance for Italy and what it means to be an ally", he said after meeting crews with Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas.

Kaunas said on social media the drone carried an explosive.

The Lithuanian Army shared video from the site of the crash, showing debris scattered in the grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made of wood and some appeared charred.

A drone alert had been issued in the ‌Lithuanian capital Vilnius and Kaunas and the surrounding regions after ​the drone was detected.

DRONE ALERT

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace ​in the Baltic region in recent months. ​Kyiv says they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming.

This has stoked ‌concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling ​over NATO's borders.

Fighters with the ​NATO Baltic Air Defence mission have patrolled the skies of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia since the Baltic countries joined the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray Ukrainian drones over ​Estonia in May, and over Latvia in ‌June and August.

Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russia, including in the Baltic ​Sea area.

(Reporting by Andrius Sytas in Vilnius, Tom Balmforth in London, Janis Laizans in ​Siauliai; Editing by Stephen Coates, Timothy Heritage, Ros Russell)
